title: Inversion-symmetric topological insulators in cut-and-project binary chains
authors: Zhipeng Zeng, Yuge Chen, Jean-Noël Fuchs, Jianxin Zhong, Rémy Mosseri
abstract: We investigate the electronic properties of binary tight-binding chains generated by the cut-and-project method for rational slopes $α=p/q$, leading to periodic and inversion symmetric chains with $n=p+q$ sites. The binary structure is encoded in two hopping amplitudes $t_a$ and $t_b$. For fixed $t_a \neq t_b$, the support of the energy spectrum as a function of $p/n$ gives rise to a "Cut-and-Project butterfly". We concentrate on insulators with $M$ filled bands among a total of $n$ bands and vary $t_a/t_b$. Inversion symmetry constrains the electric polarization $P$ to $0$ or $P_q/2$ modulo a polarization quantum $P_q = \gcd(M,n)/n$. A topological transition, between two insulators that differ by their quantized polarization, occurs if and only if $n/\gcd(M,n)$ is odd. When $n/\gcd(M,n)$ is even, the two insulating regimes have a vanishing polarization and no topological transition occurs, despite the gap closing at $t_a=t_b$. When $n$ is even and $M$ odd, we find an adiabatic path between $t_a>t_b$ and $t_a<t_b$ that maintains inversion symmetry and a gap.
summary: This work analyzes topological insulators in 1D chains created via the cut-and-project method, which imposes inversion symmetry. The authors establish a precise mathematical criterion—related to the ratio $n/\gcd(M,n)$—that dictates whether a topological transition occurs between different insulating phases. This provides a deep theoretical understanding of how lattice geometry and band filling control topological behavior.
main_problem: The paper investigates the electronic properties and topological transitions in inversion-symmetric topological insulators constructed using the cut-and-project method for binary chains.
main_result: Topological transitions are strictly governed by an arithmetic criterion: they occur if and only if $n/\gcd(M,n)$ is odd, with specific exceptions noted for even values.
method: The analysis employs tight-binding models derived from the cut-and-project method, utilizing symmetry constraints (inversion symmetry) and topological diagnostics like the Zak phase and polarization.
model_or_system: The system is a one-dimensional periodic chain with a binary hopping structure ($t_A, t_B$), generated by projecting a 2D lattice structure ($\mathbb{Z}^2$) via the cut-and-project method for rational slopes $\alpha=p/q$.
key_observables: Electric polarization ($P$), topological transition points, and the energy spectrum visualized as a "Cut-and-Project butterfly".
important_parameters: The hopping ratio $t_A/t_B$, the number of sites $n=p+q$, and the number of filled bands $M$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to rational slopes $\alpha = p/q$, and the model assumes spinless electrons with a single orbital per site.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the CP construction, the "CP butterfly" spectrum vs. rescaled slope, and plots showing polarization jumps confirming the arithmetic criterion.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the CP model and its inherent symmetry, establishing the Hamiltonian and spectral features, and then deriving the necessary and sufficient conditions for topological transitions based on the periodicity parameters $n$ and $M$.
why_interesting: The rigorous connection between the topological invariants (polarization jumps) and simple arithmetic properties ($n/\gcd(M,n)$ parity) provides a powerful, model-independent tool for classifying topological phases in engineered quantum materials.

Bot- tom: In the present work, the selected points in the strip are instead projected onto a line of slope unity, leading to A, B bonds of equal length.

FIG. 2. CP butterfly for the binary tight-binding chains. For each rational slope α = p/q, the unit cell contains n = p + q sites and the spectrum contains n bands. The spectrum support is plotted against the rescaled CP slope θ = p/n, for hopping amplitudes tB = 1 and tA = 0.5. This diagram displays a rich hierarchical structure.

FIG. 3. Wannier-center configurations for odd and even chains. (a) α = 1/2 ABB chain: Wanniers centers sit either at a site (shared by two B bonds) or at a bond center (here an A bond); (b) α = 1/3 ABBB chain: the Wannier centers remain bond-centered in both insulating regimes, but occupy different inversion-symmetric positions (here a A bond or a B bond centers).

FIG. 4. Band structures for the chain corresponding to p/q = 2/3. The hopping amplitudes are tA = 1+δ and tB = 1−δ (a) δ < 0 and (b) δ > 0. The numbers ±1 at the high-symmetry points k = 0 and k = π label the inversion eigenvalues of each band. For bands coloured red, the product of inversion eigenvalues is ξk=0ξk=π = −1, corresponding to a Zak phase of π; for bands coloured blue, the product is +1,corresponding to a Zak phase of 0. The gaps close at δ = 0.
FIG. 5. Band structure of two odd n cases : α = 1/2, ABB (a) and α = 2/3, ABABB (b), plotted as a function of δ, with tB = 1 −δ and tA = 1 + δ. At δ = 0 the gaps close.
